P1m: I am asking people to talk about the core issues of life: jealousy, God, death, childhood, money, sex, psychedelics, and what happens when somebody wants to leave. The strange thing is, a lot of intelligent adults would much rather talk about solar panels for six hours.
P2m: This does not surprise me, since we are taught to put on a show of competence in modern society. We have a lot of incentives to hide ourselves in our lives and disappear behind our screens the second things get uncomfortable. We have been encouraged by our institutions to be narrow in our skills, and then they act surprised when nobody can sit through a conflict without appointing a subcommittee or blocking somebody.
P3m: So instead of asking "Is this person good enough?", some very practical questions to ask might be, "How much attention can this person bring to other people right now? How available is he or she to engage in self-examination? And how available are we to this person, without being consumed by him or her?"
P4m: Some people have engaged in long practices of contemplation or therapy, or have had very good luck in childhood; other people are just trying to survive some emergency in their life and need care more than responsibility. Most of us are all of these at different times in our lives.
P5m: In the model I’m imagining, some of the functions that are outsourced to therapists in modern society are distributed throughout the community. In other words, there’s a lot of peer counseling going on, people listening to each other and helping each other process ordinary emotional stuff.
P7m: I’m going to use the phrase “free resource,” which comes from Re-evaluation Counseling, to refer to the attention, steadiness and practical skill people have left over for others once they’ve dealt with enough of their own immediate stuff, and “need” to refer to the amount of help people need at a given time.
P8m: Everyone has a certain amount of both, and the ratio varies.
P11m: A group can only absorb as much need as its members have free resource to meet. The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group may end up spending most of its attention caring for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the same need can often be spread across lots of relationships and roles.
P12m: So it’s partly a problem of resources, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?
P13m: There is a difficult paradox to consider. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to tolerate the disruption of new members is less. Even with only eight people in the community, someone still has to grow the food, fix the equipment, balance the books, watch the kids, and maintain the water system. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful a new member’s heart is.
P14m: Early on, members usually need to have more resource than need, and some skill to contribute, and a willingness to learn.
P15m: How to use the framing of “I don’t have the capacity to…” without it becoming a respectable way to exclude disabled people, poor people, less articulate people, people who don’t have the language of therapy at their fingertips, people who are simply not convenient – I don’t know. It’s not going to be solved by pretending it’s unlimited; that’s going to require actually making concrete criteria, allowing for outside review, allowing for re-visiting a “not now” decision, and all of that. And even then, the power is dangerous.
P16m: You may not be a good fit for this community right now if:
L1m: You’re running from an active crisis and mainly need a place to land, get treatment, housing, legal aid, etc. (A founding group shouldn’t pretend it can replace those.)
L2m: You want all of the benefits of village life but don’t want to take on governance, maintenance, conflict, care, etc.
L3m: You’re not willing to look at yourself when jealousy or conflict comes up.
L4m: You have a need that far outstrips your ability to bring in a resource for it right now. (This doesn’t mean you’re bad or doomed, it’s about timing; it may mean you need to take a first step of finding support where you are so you can build up your resources a bit.)
P17m: (A humane membership process should have ways of not flat-out rejecting people who fall into these categories, like saying “later,” “in another role,” or “with more support.”)
